claims.claim: Hand-loading a ship cost $5.86 a ton at the time; loading via containers cost only 16 cents a ton.
claims.episode_span: those boxes had cut the cost of loading a ton of cargo from roughly $5 to less than 50 cents
claims.supporting_quote: Hand-loading a ship cost $5.86 a ton at that time. Using containers, it cost only 16 cents a ton to load a ship, 36-fold savings.

claims.claim: Malcom McLean, an American trucking businessman born in Maxton, North Carolina, invented the modern intermodal shipping container.
claims.episode_span: Malcolm McLean was a North Carolina trucker who spent the early 1950s watching freight sit for days at the docks
claims.supporting_quote: was an American businessman who invented the modern intermodal shipping container , which revolutionized transport and international trade during the second half of the twentieth century.

claims.claim: Sea-Land began transatlantic container service in April 1966 and was invited by the US government in 1967 to start a container service to South Vietnam.
claims.episode_span: by 1966 Sea-Land was running weekly service between the U.S. East Coast and Europe. The U.S. military adopted the system during the Vietnam buildup
claims.supporting_quote: In April 1966, Sea-Land commenced service between New York and Rotterdam , Netherlands; Bremen , Germany; and Grangemouth , Scotland. In 1967, Sea-Land was invited by the U.S. government to start a container service to South Vietnam .

claims.claim: London's docks could not accommodate the larger vessels containerization required; shipping moved to deep-water ports such as Tilbury and Felixstowe, and between 1960 and 1980 all of London's docks closed.
claims.episode_span: Piers built for break-bulk cargo — narrow finger piers along Manhattan, the London docks, the waterfront of San Francisco — could not accommodate the new equipment
claims.supporting_quote: London's docks were unable to accommodate the much larger vessels needed by containerization, and the shipping industry moved to deep-water ports such as Tilbury and Felixstowe . Between 1960 and 1980, all of London's docks were closed, leaving around eight square miles (21 km 2 ) of derelict land in East London.

claims.claim: New York longshore employment collapsed after containerization: employed longshoremen fell from over 50,000 in 1953 to 23,000 in 1967 and under 16,000 by the mid-1970s.
claims.episode_span: Employment on the old waterfront collapsed; the number of men working New York's piers fell by well over half within two decades of the container's arrival.
claims.source_title: Effects of automation in the lives of longshoremen - libcom.org
claims.supporting_quote: In New York, then the busiest port in the world, the number of employed longshoremen declined from over 50,000 in 1953 to 23,000 in 1967. Since then the number has dropped to under 16,000.
